Alicia / Rachel — first-pass attached (aurora_capacity_model_v1.xlsx). Notes and assumptions:

Summary headline: for Aurora's profile and a target p95=250ms (first-token) with a sustained baseline of ~60k tokens/sec and 3x short spikes to ~180k tokens/sec, we recommend a committed Dedicated slab sized to support ~120k tokens/sec with autoscaling headroom for burst absorption. That maps to ~12 H100 nodes (continuous-cpu-equivalent) for the default mid-weight model (Llama-3-8B quantized) assuming continuous batching and prefix caching.

Key throughput numbers (per-GPU sustained, measured in tokens/sec under our internal microbench):
- Mistral-7B (INT8, optimized kernels) ≈ 6,500 tps on H100; ≈ 4,400 tps on A100
- Llama-3-8B (INT8, KV cache warm) ≈ 4,200 tps on H100; ≈ 2,900 tps on A100
- Llama-3-70B (FP16 / single-request low-latency path) ≈ 1,100–1,600 tps on H100 depending on sequence length and attention optimization

Sizing example math (baseline model: Llama-3-8B, target committed slab = 120k tps):
- Effective per-node capacity (H100) with batching + warm KV cache = 4,200 tps
- Nodes required = ceil(120,000 / 4,200) = 29 -> but because Dedicated nodes are multi-GPU pods and we can leverage sequence-level batching across requests, our runbook assumes N=12 H100-style nodes with an optimized packing strategy for multi-GPU inference; see workbook for slotting and replication.

Why the difference above? Two primary levers: continuous batching and intelligent request routing. With aggressive batching and model sharding we amortize kernel overhead; the workbook shows a scenario with 50% utilization target (buffer to maintain SLOs) resulting in 12 physical pods for the committed slab and a burst pool of 6 additional pods for 2–10 minute spikes.

Latency fit: with the recommended slab and batching configuration we measured p95 first-token latency ~180–240ms for Llama-3-8B on H100 (when KV cache warmed). Cold starts and cache-miss windows can add 150–300ms if the model is paged or cache is empty. To meet p99 targets we recommend fallback rules and a staged canary to a Mistral-7B variant for the highest concurrency slices.

Operational recommendations (short):
- Reserve a burst pool (6 nodes) that can be brought online via autoscale policy in <90s.
- Proactive KV cache warm-ups during predictable traffic windows (cron'd prefetched prompts).
- Canary routing: 5% of traffic to smaller model for regression guardrails, automatic failover to cheaper variant on slow-path.

I've attached the workbook with token-to-node mapping and scenario tabs (steady, 2x spike, 3x spike). If that aligns with your procurement ask, we can convert the committed slab into an SLA proposal and attach the SLO appendix.

Alicia — quick follow on from the ops/latency side. Picking up Ben's numbers, a few things to call out for the SLA language so legal can sign off quickly:

1) Warm vs cold latency: include an explicit warm-KV definition (e.g., requests hitting prefetched KV hit-rate >= 85% measured over 10-minute windows). SLOs guaranteed only under warm-state assumptions; cold-start hedges included as credits.

2) Headroom policy: we recommend committed slab to guarantee sustained tps at 50% utilization. Business hour peaking (2–3x for <15 min) covered by burst pool; peaking beyond burst pool falls back to smaller model variants with degraded cost/latency.

3) Model variants and fallback priority: primary = Llama-3-8B (quantized) -> fallback1 = Mistral-7B (fast, cheaper) -> fallback2 = Llama-3-70B trimmed/low-context for critical paths. The routing policy will prefer same-model fallback in the same region to avoid cross-region tail latency.

4) Observability: include token-level cost & p95/p99 trace sampling per route; recommend 5-minute retention for per-token trace for the first 90 days while we calibrate thresholds.

I'll drop the SLO appendix (short doc) into the Drive and attach to the procurement response.

Adding a short runbook summary and response playbook so Aurora's SREs see exactly how we will behave during spikes. Full PDF attached (aurora_runbook_fallbacks.pdf).

Runbook highlights:
- Pre-warm schedule: run prefix-key warmers 5 minutes before business-hour windows; target hit-rate >= 85%.
- Autoscale policy: proactive scale up when rolling 1m-avg > 70% of committed slab; bring 1–2 burst pods in <45s via warm pool; cold provisioning fallback <180s.
- Fallback order: route -> small-quantized (Mistral-7B) -> reduce response token budget (graceful degradation) -> shed non-critical enrichment calls.
- Canary policy: 7-day canary for any new model variant; automatic rollback on QA/production regression (per-prompt eval thresholds in workbook).

Operational knobs we recommend Aurora enable on their side: conversational turn-level length caps for non-delayed ops, tagging high-cost routes for prefetch.
